pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Arabic name of the temple town

phonemes.desc: From Arabic al-uqsur, “the palaces/castles” — the Arab name for the temple ruins of Thebes’ east bank.
Ancient Egyptian: Ipet-resyt, “the Southern Sanctuary” — the harem of Amun.

pronunciation.note: A medieval Arabic plural fossilised into a modern proper name — the “palaces” the Arabs found.

domains.title: The Palaces, the Southern Sanctuary
domains.subtitle: Ipet-resyt, the Harem of Amun
domains.lead: Luxor — Arabic ‘the palaces’ — names the southern sanctuary of the Theban triad, where Amun visited in the great Opet festival to renew his generative power. Its ancient name, Ipet-resyt, ‘the Southern Select Place’, marks it as Karnak’s counterpart across the river: not the god’s estate but his bridal-chamber.

cards.name: The Southern Sanctuary
cards.desc: Ipet-resyt — the harem-temple where Amun’s fertility was renewed each year.

cards.name: The Birth Colonnade
cards.desc: Reliefs of the divine birth of Amenhotep III — the king’s theology of legitimate succession.

cards.name: The Colonnade of Amenhotep III
cards.desc: Fourteen massive papyrus columns — the finest preserved New Kingdom colonnade.

cards.name: Opet’s Destination
cards.desc: The river-end of the great festival: Amun’s barque docked here for the marriage-renewal rites.

mythology.lead: Luxor’s mythology is the fertility-cycle of Amun himself: each year the god sailed south from Karnak to his harem at Ipet-resyt, married his own power in the sanctuary, and returned renewed. The temple’s birth-colonnade extends the cycle to kingship — Amenhotep III’s divine conception carved as theology-in-stone.

myths.title: The Southern Journey
myths.text: The Opet festival’s climax was the god’s arrival at Ipet-resyt: the barque of Amun moored before the colonnade, the Theban crowd celebrating the union that renewed the Nile, the king, and the year in a single night of liturgy. The return to Karnak closed the cycle eleven days later.

myths.title: Amun and Mutemwiya
myths.text: Luxor’s colonnade reliefs narrate the conception of Amenhotep III: Amun takes the form of the king, visits queen Mutemwiya, the child is fashioned by Khnum on the potter’s wheel and blessed by the gods — the canonical statement that the pharaoh is the god’s literal son, carved at full scale.

myths.title: The Sanctuary Continuous
myths.text: A mosque still stands inside the temple’s court — Abu Haggag of Luxor, whose mouloud festival each year crowds the ancient colonnade with boats and lights. The building has never stopped being sacred; only the name of the sacred changed, from Ipet-resyt to the Sheikh’s mosque.

myths.title: The Palaces
myths.text: The Arabs who settled among the ruins called them al-uqsur — ‘the castles’ — seeing palaces in the pylons; the name shrank to Luxor and became the city’s. It is one of the few cases where the medieval name of the ruins replaced the ancient name of the living town.

lore.syncretism: Luxor temple served Amun in his ithyphallic generative form — Amun-Min-Kamutef, ‘bull of his mother’ — tying the sanctuary to Min’s fertility theology. Its chapels later honoured the Roman imperial cult, then the mosque of Abu Haggag: three religions in one floor-plan, each claiming the same consecrated ground.
lore.culturalLegacy: The colonnade of Amenhotep III, floodlit on the Nile’s corniche, is the most photographed temple front in the world after the Pyramids. The birth-colonnade’s iconography — Khnum at the potter’s wheel, the divine child — became the standard visual argument of Egyptian kingship, copied in every royal birth-chapel of the New Kingdom.
lore.extendedMeditation: Luxor: a medieval plural doing the work of an ancient sanctuary-name. In the lexicon it stands for the archaeological truth that places outlive their theologies — ‘the palaces’ the Arabs named are the same walls where Amun’s fertility was renewed, and the name needs no restoration because it never referred to anything but the stones themselves.

sources.name: Opet festival reliefs and barque-docking scenes
Haeny, Luxor in the Oxford Encyclopedia of Ancient Egypt

lore.archaeology: Amenhotep III’s colonnade and court survive at near-perfect scale; the pylon of Ramesses II fronts it with its single obelisk — the other stands in Paris’ Place de la Concorde. The temple’s axis was recently realigned with the re-excavated Avenue of Sphinxes to Karnak, restoring the ancient processional road.
lore.cult: The temple was the stage of the Opet marriage-rites and the cult of Amun-Min; its priests served the ‘Southern Sanctuary’ as Karnak’s served the northern estate. The medieval mosque kept the ground consecrated without interruption — a continuity unmatched in the ancient world.
lore.iconography: The papyrus-bundle columns of the colonnade, the seated colossi of Ramesses II, the barque-shrine of Amun; and above all the birth-scenes’ sequence — embrace, conception, fashioning on the wheel. The icon of Luxor is procession arriving: the god’s boat at the stair.
lore.reception: Luxor is modern Egypt’s tourist capital and the ancient world’s best-preserved large temple front. Its obelisk in Paris made it the first Egyptian monument to join a European capital’s furniture; and the mouloud of Abu Haggag is studied worldwide as the longest-lived case of continuous sacred use of one building.
